fact_text: A third-country national relocated to Malta for employment of more than six months applies for a Single Permit, a combined work-and-residence authorisation regulated by Subsidiary Legislation 217.17; the single application procedure incorporates both an employment licence and a residence permit.
evidence_quote: authorises third country nationals to legally reside and take up employment in Malta for a defined period of over 6 months

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a work visa and a residence visa are two separate filings. Actually Malta issues ONE combined Single Permit (SL 217.17) covering both work and residence. Action: submit a single combined application through the employer, not separate work and residence applications.

entity_title: Permit tied to employer and role
fact_text: A Maltese Single Permit is issued specifically for the named employer and job designation shown on the residence document; any change to either renders the permit null and void, regardless of the expiry date printed on it, and requires a fresh application.
evidence_quote: Any changes occurring in either of these criteria render the permit null and void, irrespective of the date validity showing on the same document and necessitate a new application.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the permit stays valid until its printed expiry even if you switch employer or role. Actually any change of employer or designation voids it immediately, whatever the expiry date. Action: do not begin a new role or employer until a new Single Permit application is approved.

fact_text: The employment-based residence card issued to a third-country national prints the specific designation, employer and duration on which the permit was granted, and the permit is valid only while those criteria continue to be met.
evidence_quote: the specific designation, employer and duration. This information is also printed on the residence card issued and held by the third-country national.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the residence card is a generic ID showing only identity and validity dates. Actually it prints your exact employer, designation and duration, and the permit holds only while those remain true. Action: keep the card's details in sync with your real job and report any change to Identita.

entity_title: No EU free movement for work
fact_text: A Maltese residence permit based on employment does not give the holder any right to move to and work in other EU member states; the employment must be located in Malta.
evidence_quote: the holding of a residence permit does not give the holder the right of movement within the EU in terms of employment.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a residence permit from one EU country lets you work anywhere in the EU. Actually a Maltese employment residence permit is Malta-only and confers no EU labour mobility. Action: treat any onward EU assignment as a separate immigration process in that country.

fact_text: Subsidiary Legislation 217.17 allows up to four months to process a Single Permit application, though Identita's stated average is closer to two months from submission of a complete application accompanied by all required documents.
evidence_quote: Subsidiary Legislation 217.17 allows four (4) months for the processing of a Single Permit application, however the average processing time is closer to two (2) months

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a work permit is issued within days or a couple of weeks. Actually the statutory processing window is up to four months (averaging about two). Action: plan the relocation start date roughly two to four months after a complete Single Permit submission.

fact_text: The work component of the Single Permit is an employment licence: every Single Permit application filed with Identita is referred to Jobsplus, which conducts labour-market tests and reviews from an employment perspective before the permit can issue.
evidence_quote: referred to Jobsplus to conduct the necessary labour market tests and reviews from an employment perspective

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed Identita alone decides the permit. Actually Jobsplus is a mandatory stakeholder that runs a labour-market test on every Single Permit before issuance. Action: prepare for a Jobsplus employment-side review, not only an immigration review.

fact_text: Before a third-country national can be employed, the employer must first search the Maltese and EU/EEA labour market and advertise the vacancy to demonstrate that no qualified Maltese or EU/EEA candidate is available for the position.
evidence_quote: This search aims to ensure that no qualified candidate from Malta and/or the EU/EEA is available for the vacant position. Employers must advertise the job vacancy to comply with these requirements.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed an employer can hire a chosen foreign candidate directly. Actually a labour-market test requires advertising the role first to prove no Malta/EU/EEA candidate is available. Action: run and document the EU-preference job advertisement before filing.

fact_text: It is illegal to employ the third-country national before the Single Permit is issued; only once the permit is granted may the employer register the engagement with Jobsplus through an engagement form.
evidence_quote: It is illegal to employ the TCN prior to the issuance of the permit / approval.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you can start work once the application is filed or a start date is agreed. Actually employing the person before the permit issues is illegal. Action: set the employment start date only after the Single Permit is granted.

fact_text: The Key Employee Initiative fast-track is open to third-country nationals offered a managerial or highly technical position; eligibility requires proof of an annual gross salary of at least EUR 45,000 plus the relevant qualifications, warrants or work experience.
evidence_quote: an annual gross salary of at least €45,000 per annum

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed any skilled hire qualifies for Malta's fast-track. Actually the KEI requires a managerial or highly technical role AND a gross salary of at least EUR 45,000 per annum. Action: confirm the offered salary meets the EUR 45,000 KEI floor before relying on the 5-day route.

fact_text: For eligible highly skilled hires the Key Employee Initiative fast-tracks the Single Permit to an expected processing time of five working days, counted once a complete application with all checklist documents is submitted online.
evidence_quote: KEI applications expected processing time is five (5) working days from the submission of the application.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the fast-track is only marginally quicker. Actually the KEI targets about five working days versus the standard up-to-four-months Single Permit. Action: if role and salary qualify, apply under KEI to compress the timeline dramatically.

fact_text: Skilled third-country nationals who do not meet the KEI threshold may use the Specialist Employee Initiative, an alternative Single Permit route targeting those earning at least EUR 25,000 per annum in specific positions with qualifications at MQF level 6 or higher (or MQF certification plus three years of experience).
evidence_quote: skilled individuals and will be earning at least €25,000 per annum

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed there is only one skilled-worker fast route (the KEI). Actually the SEI is a separate route for those below the KEI bar, needing about EUR 25,000 salary and MQF level 6 qualifications. Action: if salary is under the EUR 45,000 KEI floor, check SEI eligibility instead.
